page: Microsoft Azure E16d_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance based on the x86_64 architecture. It provides 16 vCPUs derived from 8 dedicated physical cores running on an Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C processor clocked at 2.8 GHz, supported by 48 MB of L3 cache. Hyper-threading is enabled with two threads per core. Memory allocation stands at 128.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio (8.0 GB per core). For temporary storage needs, the instance includes 644 GB of direct-attached local SSD storage. The platform operates on Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization and does not include discrete GPU hardware accelerators.

Benchmark measurements position the E16d_v5 solidly within the middle tier across compute and memory workloads. The instance achieves a Geekbench single-core score of 1638.0 and a multi-core score of 9964.0, while PassMark tests record an aggregate CPU score of 21390.9 and a memory score of 2745.32. Vector instructions including AVX-512 and AVX-512 VNNI support parallel processing tasks, registering 14725.03 in the PassMark extended instructions test. Memory bandwidth reaches 96.81 GB/sec for uncached 256 MB read blocks and 56.93 GB/sec for writes. In application-focused metrics, it yields 14.9 million operations per second in Redis SET tests and 21.56 GB/sec in static web serving throughput.

The presence of 644 GB local SSD storage paired with a high memory footprint makes the E16d_v5 resource-dense for memory-bound tasks requiring rapid local scratch space. Cost efficiency is defined by the high ratio of RAM to vCPU, avoiding the need to over-provision compute cores solely to obtain substantial memory capacity. However, as an x86 configuration without hardware GPUs, it is constrained to lighter CPU-based machine learning inference, where it manages 11.63 tokens per second generating text on a 7B model.

Microsoft Azure E16d_v5 fits enterprise workloads including in-memory caching layers such as Redis, relational and NoSQL transactional databases, medium-scale data analytics, compilation pipelines, and memory-intensive web application servers.
